title: Marine Exposure Performance of a Circular-Concrete Floating Breakwater Prototype: Biofouling, Chloride Ingress and Structural Monitoring
content: Field evidence on the performance of circular concrete materials in floating marine structures remains limited. This study presents the design, manufacture and nine-month marine exposure of a reduced-scale floating breakwater prototype measuring 3.40 m × 1.70 m × 1.05 m at the Port of Gijón, Spain. The reinforced shell comprised high-performance concrete in the bottom slab and walls and lightweight aggregate concrete in the top slab, while the core combined cellular concrete with fully encapsulated expanded polystyrene required to satisfy the buoyancy constraints of the reduced-scale prototype. The structure was held in position by a four-line catenary mooring system connected to gravity anchors.Prototype performance was evaluated through biofouling surveys, embedded corrosion-potential measurements, chloride profiling, reinforcement inspection, eddy-current corrosion sensing and acceleration monitoring. Biofouling coverage exceeded 85% on all evaluated surfaces, with mussel-dominated layers up to 35 mm thick. Wet biomass on the two sampled lateral faces ranged from 6.3 to 9.7 kg/m². Highly negative reinforcement potentials at permanently submerged locations were consistent with water-saturated, oxygen-limited concrete and did not, in isolation, demonstrate active corrosion. Chloride content exceeded the applicable 0.6% code limit at reinforcement depth only in the lightweight-concrete top slab near openings introduced for monitoring equipment. Possible localised pitting was observed in this area, but no measurable reduction in reinforcement thickness was detected.Environmental compensation reduced the variability of the eddy-current baseline to a ±135 Ω reference band during the analysed period, although field detection of active corrosion was not demonstrated. Dominant measured frequencies of 0.35–0.45 Hz were broadly consistent, within the estimated ±20% uncertainty, with the calculated rigid-body natural-frequency range, particularly the heave and pitch estimates.The campaign demonstrated satisfactory short-term marine performance of the prototype and identified instrumentation openings as the most critical durability details. The results also provide field evidence on biological colonisation, chloride ingress and sensor operation in a floating circular-concrete structure. Longer exposure under open-sea conditions is required to assess lifecycle durability, corrosion development and the long-term effects of biofouling on hydrodynamic response and mooring loads.
